metadata.title: Profit and Loss Across Multiple Articles
metadata.description: Combine transactions correctly by adding total costs and total receipts rather than averaging percentage rates blindly.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the commercial relationship step by step, explain why each rate uses its base, show intermediate amounts, check signs and units, then practice transfer with misconception-specific retries.
metadata.sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 12 “Profit and Loss,” printed pages 374–425. Approved scope: Find the net result for several items sold at different gains or losses. Add each item's CP and SP (or profit/loss amount) and calculate the overall percentage using total CP as the base. Explain weighted results and why a simple mean of percentages is generally wrong. Include unequal costs, different margins, same or different sale prices, and a check that the combined rate lies consistently with the component amounts. Use chapter objective patterns involving multiple devices, goods, lots, and combined receipts.

content.text: Profit and Loss Across Multiple Articles: Combine transactions correctly by adding total costs and total receipts rather than averaging percentage rates blindly. We establish the model, explain each step, and practice with targeted feedback.
When several items are sold, add their costs and add their receipts. Overall profit is total SP−total CP; overall loss is the reverse. The percentage then uses total CP.
A simple mean of individual profit rates is usually wrong because the items can have different costs. A 20% return on ₹100 contributes ₹20, while 20% on ₹1,000 contributes ₹200.
Example: one article costs ₹500 and gains 20%; another costs ₹1,500 and loses 10%. Receipts are ₹600 and ₹1,350, so totals are CP ₹2,000 and SP ₹1,950: net loss ₹50, or 2.5%.
Weight each rate by its cost: overall profit fraction=(sum of CP_i×rate_i)/sum CP_i, with losses entered as negative rates. This is equivalent to adding currency results directly.
If identical articles have the same CP, the arithmetic mean of their rates does work because the costs are equal weights. State that condition before using an average shortcut.
Equal selling prices do not imply equal costs. An item sold at a gain has a lower CP than the receipt; an item sold at a loss has a higher CP.

If the same SP is received for two articles, recover each CP from its own factor. Then compare total SP with total CP. This avoids the misleading intuition that equal sales amounts mean equal margins.
If costs and profit/loss amounts are supplied, do not convert every rate first. Add total CP and total profit/loss; the overall rate is a single final division.

If profit percentages are given on different bases (for example, a profit rate on one item’s CP and a loss rate on another item’s SP), translate each statement into currency amounts before aggregating.
A group transaction can be profitable even if one item loses money. The question asks the combined result, so each gain and loss belongs in the same ledger.
Check the result against the component margins. A larger-cost item should influence the overall rate more strongly than a low-cost item.
For same CP and equal x% gain and x% loss, receipts total 2CP and the net difference is zero only if the losses are measured on an equal CP. Do not confuse this with equal SP.
When total CP is missing but total SP and net result are known, set the equation directly. For example, profit=SP−CP and profit%=profit/CP.
Keep rounding until the end if rates are recurring. An early rounded individual profit can shift the final combined amount by several currency units.
A reliable final check is to reconstruct each item’s SP from CP and its signed rate, add those receipts, and compare the sum with the reported overall rate.
